title: Yarrow
subtitle: The wound herb: compresses, washes, and fever infusions from the hedgerow
excerpt: Yarrow is a common hedgerow plant whose feathery leaves and flat-topped flower clusters have been used as a first-aid herb for minor cuts, grazes, and nosebleeds across European and Native American traditions. The dried aerial parts are prepared as a compress for wounds, a wash for oily or congested skin, and a hot infusion taken to support the body during a mild fever. Dried yarrow keeps 12 months in a tin.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), yarrow entry, Botanical.com transcription. Nicholas Culpeper, Complete Herbal (1653), yarrow entry, public domain. EMA HMPC Community herbal monograph on Achillea millefolium L. herba (2009, EMA/HMPC/302849/2009), open access. Felter & Lloyd, King's American Dispensatory (1898), Achillea entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or substance that, when applied to a minor wound, helps slow bleeding by constricting small blood vessels locally.
A herb traditionally taken as a hot infusion to encourage mild sweating, used in western herbal practice to support the body during the early stage of a fever.

content.text: Yarrow in the home medicine cupboard, dried aerial parts for a compress on a minor cut, a wash for blemish-prone skin, or a hot infusion taken at the onset of a mild fever. A herb with one of the longest documented first-aid uses in European tradition, long gathered from hedgerows and meadows for minor wounds and the early, sweaty phase of a cold. A jar of dried yarrow keeps 12 months. the herb is easily grown or gathered where positively identified.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Achillea millefolium L., family Asteraceae. A perennial herb, 20 to 80 cm, with finely divided, feathery leaves, the 'millefolium' (thousand-leaved) of the name, and flat-topped clusters of small white or pale pink flower heads from early summer through autumn. Found in meadows, roadsides, and dry grassland across Europe, Asia, and North America. The aerial parts, leaves, stems, and flowers, are used. Harvest during or just before flowering, when the volatile oil content is highest.

Identification caution: the feathery leaf is a yarrow signature, but hemlock can produce superficially similar leaf shapes in young plants. Hemlock has a distinctive unpleasant mousy smell when crushed, hollow stems with purple-red blotches, and grows taller (up to 2 m). Yarrow stems are solid and the leaf smells faintly pleasant and aromatic. If in any doubt, do not gather, use supplier-sourced dried herb.

The aerial parts carry a volatile oil rich in chamazulene (in the blue-oil chemotype), camphor, and borneol. flavonoids including luteolin and apigenin. achilleine (a styptic compound). sesquiterpene lactones. and tannins. The
action on minor wounds is well documented in the traditional literature. The
action, taken as a hot infusion at the start of a fever, is one of the core fever-management strategies in the western herbal tradition.

The name Achillea refers to the legend that Achilles used yarrow to staunch wounds on the Trojan battlefield. Whether or not the story is true, yarrow's use as a wound herb is among the oldest documented in European herbalism. the 17th-century herbalist Culpeper recommended it for "all manner of bleeding" and for wounds. the 20th-century herbalist Grieve gives detailed guidance for nosebleeds, minor cuts, and the fever use. The Eclectic-American tradition used yarrow as a sweat-inducing in fevers and for urinary tract conditions. The current European herbal guidance reference entry supports traditional use for minor skin inflammation and as a wound herb.

Strong infusion for compress: 2 tablespoons of dried yarrow per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 10 to 15 minutes, strained. Soak a clean cloth in the cooled liquid and apply to the minor wound or area for 10 to 20 minutes.

Hot infusion for fever support: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried yarrow per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 8 to 10 minutes, strained, and drunk as hot as comfortable. One to two cups taken during the early, cold-and-shivery stage of a mild fever.
Asteraceae allergy: yarrow belongs to the daisy family. If you have a confirmed allergy to ragweed or chamomile, avoid yarrow. Cross-reactions are common within this plant family.
Pregnancy: do not use. Yarrow has traditional use as a uterine stimulant and to promote menstrual flow, and Current safety guidance advises against use in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Wound use limits: yarrow on a minor graze or clean cut is appropriate home treatment. A wound that is deep, contaminated, heavily bleeding, or shows signs of infection (red spreading borders, warmth, pus) needs medical assessment, not herbal first aid.
